interview_metadata.name: Deeva Cintron
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Oh my, that is a big question. Well, let me settle in. I was born in 1940, in Adrian, Michigan — a little farming town about forty miles southwest of here. My people were German stock, second generation. My grandfather Otto came over from Baden before the first war, and my father grew up speaking a little German at home, though he dropped it quick when the second war started because it wasn't popular to sound German then. I was the oldest of four. My father worked at the Bohn Aluminum plant and my mother kept the house, put up preserves, sewed our clothes on a treadle Singer. We had a vegetable garden every year — I still garden because of her, honestly. Church was First Methodist, twice on Sundays and Wednesday prayer meeting, and the Ladies' Aid society practically raised me alongside my mother. I went to Adrian High, graduated in 1958, and then I did two years at Siena Heights studying business administration. I didn't finish — I met my husband Harold at a church social my sophomore year, he was working at Ford's Ypsilanti plant, and we married in 1961. We moved to Saline because Harold's supervisor lived here and said it was a decent town with good schools. I was a full-time homemaker for most of our marriage, though I kept the books for Harold's side business doing small engine repair out of the garage, and I did the treasurer work for the church women's group for almost thirty years. We had three children — Kathy in '62, Daniel in '64, and Rebecca in '68. Harold passed away in 2019, heart attack, and that was the hardest thing. Since then I've kept at the garden, the quilting, the bridge group, and I volunteer at the library's reading hour and at the senior center doing their bookkeeping. That's the short version of eighty-five years.

follow_ups.question: What do you remember most vividly from your childhood?
follow_ups.response: Canning season. End of August, my mother and her sisters would come over and we'd do twenty, thirty quarts of tomatoes in a day, the windows fogged up with steam and the pressure cooker hissing. I still can my own sauerkraut every fall because of it.

follow_ups.question: You said meeting Harold was at a church social — what do you remember about that night?
follow_ups.response: He was wearing a blue shirt with the collar frayed and he asked me if I knew how to play euchre. I said of course, I'm from Michigan. We played three hands and he drove me home and that was it. Fifty-eight years we were married.

follow_ups.question: What was the hardest part about losing Harold?
follow_ups.response: The quiet. Harold talked to himself while he worked, and the house had a hum to it. When he went, the hum went. I still set two coffee cups out some mornings before I catch myself.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes, I think about this often. It was spring of 1960, the end of my sophomore year at Siena Heights. I had a professor, Sister Mary Agnes, who taught accounting, and she pulled me aside after an exam and said I had a real head for numbers, and that I should think about finishing the degree and sitting for the CPA exam. Harold had just proposed that Easter. I could have said to him, let me finish, let me do another two years and then a year for the exam prep. I chose the marriage instead. I told myself I'd go back when the children were in school, and I did take one night class at Washtenaw Community in 1974, but I never finished. I don't regret the marriage, not a minute of it, but sometimes when I'm balancing the senior center books in about forty-five minutes flat I wonder what I'd have been like as a CPA. That's the crossroads for me.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever tell Harold about Sister Mary Agnes's advice?
follow_ups.response: I did, years later, maybe in the eighties. He said why didn't you tell me at the time, I'd have waited. But I knew he wouldn't have, and I wouldn't have asked him to.

follow_ups.question: Do you still want to finish that degree?
follow_ups.response: I do. That's one of my goals — I'd like to finish the business admin certificate at Washtenaw. I've looked into their senior audit program. I just haven't pulled the trigger.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice, though at the time I dressed it up as what everybody did. Girls in 1961 in small-town Michigan got married and kept house. But I knew I was choosing. I sat on the porch one evening and thought it through and chose.

follow_ups.question: Do you tend to be a deliberate decision-maker in general?
follow_ups.response: Very much. I make lists. I double-check. Harold used to say I'd measure a board four times before I cut it. That's how I am.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Honestly, Sister Mary Agnes did. She gave me the chance. What I needed and didn't have was anyone saying you can do both — marry and finish. The whole culture then said pick one. A mentor who was a married working woman might've changed my mind, but I didn't know any.

follow_ups.question: Do you try to be that mentor for younger women now?
follow_ups.response: I do with my granddaughters. I tell them finish your schooling first. My granddaughter Emma is in her junior year at Grand Valley and I remind her every phone call.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I'm a widow. Harold passed in September of 2019. We have three children. Kathy is the oldest — she's sixty-three, lives in Ann Arbor with her husband Tom, she was a grade school teacher, retired now. They have two kids, my grandson Brian who's a software engineer out in Denver, and Emma who's at Grand Valley studying nursing. Then Daniel, our middle, he's sixty-one, he's out in Portland, Oregon — that's where my grandson Jacob is, he's in high school. Daniel does something with environmental engineering, water systems. He and his husband Marco have been together twenty-two years, married in 2015 when they finally could. And Rebecca, the baby, she's fifty-seven, lives in Toledo, she's a dental hygienist. She and her husband Greg have three kids — Sophie is in medical school, Caleb is at Bowling Green, and little Lily is a sophomore in high school. So three children, six grandchildren, no great-grandchildren yet though Sophie is engaged. Kathy comes up every Sunday for lunch and drives me to my appointments. Rebecca I see once a month, she comes up the first Saturday. Daniel I mostly see on video calls, once a week, Sunday evenings. That's my family.

follow_ups.question: How did you and Harold handle Daniel coming out?
follow_ups.response: Oh, that was 1986, he was twenty-two and home from college. I cried, not because I was upset at him but because I worried about his life in that time. Harold was quiet for two days, then he told Daniel that he loved him and that was that. We marched in Pride with him in Detroit in 1990, Harold in a Tigers cap looking like he wandered in by accident. I'm proud of that.

follow_ups.question: What does Sunday lunch with Kathy usually look like?
follow_ups.response: She comes at noon. I make a pot roast or a chicken pot pie, she brings a salad, we eat at the dining room table, then we do the crossword together. She leaves around three. Been the same routine since Harold died.

follow_ups.question: Tell me about your Sunday video call with Daniel.
follow_ups.response: Seven o'clock my time, four his. Marco usually pops in to say hello. Daniel walks me around his garden — they have quite a garden out there in Portland, he grows things I can't grow here. We talk about thirty minutes.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My sister Margaret — Maggie — she's eighty-two, lives in Tecumseh. We talk on the phone Tuesday and Friday mornings. My brothers are both passed. And my sister-in-law Dolores, Harold's sister, we still exchange Christmas cards.

follow_ups.question: What's a typical Tuesday call with Maggie like?
follow_ups.response: Nine o'clock sharp. Weather, grandchildren, the obituaries in the Adrian paper — we always read each other the ones we know. Fifteen minutes usually.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My bridge group — four of us. Marjorie Klein, Pat O'Donnell, and Ruth Chen. We've played Tuesday afternoons at the senior center for eleven years. Then my walking partner Eleanor from down the block, we meet Monday and Thursday mornings for the walking club behind the library. And my church friends — the fellowship group I organize, about twelve of us, we meet the second and fourth Sundays after service. Pastor Jim and his wife Sarah stop by for tea about once a month. And Ellen next door — she's sixty, still working, but she checks in on me and I keep an eye on her dog when she travels.

follow_ups.question: Who is your closest friend of all of those?
follow_ups.response: Marjorie. We've known each other since 1972 when our kids were in Boy Scouts together. She's the one I'd call at three in the morning.

follow_ups.question: How did you meet Eleanor?
follow_ups.response: She moved in across the street in 2014. I brought over a jar of my apple butter. That's how you meet neighbors.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Saline, in the older part of town off Michigan Avenue, about six blocks from downtown. Ranch houses mostly, built in the late fifties and early sixties, decent lots — mine is a third of an acre. A lot of original owners still here or their kids bought the houses back. The younger families that moved in over the last fifteen years are mostly commuters to Ann Arbor. It's quiet, sidewalks in good repair, the city plows promptly. Mill Pond Park is four blocks away. The library's a mile, I walk it in good weather. The farmers market Saturday mornings downtown is a highlight in the summer. Saline's got good bones — small town, schools are good, downtown has a hardware store, two cafes, the Stone Arch bookshop. I can walk to most things I need, which matters now that I only drive in daylight.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been in this house?
follow_ups.response: Sixty-two years this May. We bought it in 1964 for fourteen thousand dollars when Daniel was on the way.

follow_ups.question: Have you thought about downsizing?
follow_ups.response: Kathy brings it up. I won't. The garden is here, Harold planted the oak out front, and I'm not moving.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very safe. I lock my doors at night but that's habit. Saline PD is responsive, I've never had anything more than a mailbox flag broken by teenagers one Halloween. I walk alone at dusk and don't think twice.

follow_ups.question: Have you always felt this safe here?
follow_ups.response: Yes. In sixty-two years we had one break-in attempt, 1987, Harold scared him off with a flashlight. That's the tally.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Mostly up. The downs are minor — property taxes have crept up, the new subdivisions on the west side have added traffic, and the new folks don't always wave. The ups are the roots. Sixty-two years of Christmases, kids' birthdays, Harold's garage, my garden. You can't buy that.

follow_ups.question: Has Saline changed much?
follow_ups.response: More chains out by the highway, fewer farms. But downtown is holding on, the schools are still strong, and the Saline Summerfest every August is the same parade I walked my kids to in 1970.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Just me. I've been alone in the house since Harold passed in September 2019. Kathy stayed with me for two weeks after the funeral and Rebecca came up for a week in December that year, but since then, just me. I have a cat, Winston, a gray tabby I got from the humane society in 2020 to have something to talk to. He counts as household in my book but not on the census.

follow_ups.question: How did you adjust to living alone?
follow_ups.response: Slowly. First six months I didn't cook a proper meal. Then I made myself a rule — dinner at six, at the table, the good plates. Brought me back.

follow_ups.question: Tell me about Winston.
follow_ups.response: Six years old, neutered male, gray tabby, sixteen pounds — a little stout. Sits on the quilting frame when I'm working, which he's not supposed to do. Sleeps on the left side of the bed, where Harold used to.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Permanent — just me and Winston.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that.
transcript.response: Emma stays in the guest room when she's home from Grand Valley on breaks — usually Thanksgiving, Christmas, and a week in May.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, no one.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: I keep a rigid schedule, it's how I am. Up at 5:45 every day, coffee, oatmeal, Bible reading, crossword. Monday and Thursday are walking club at 8 a.m. behind the library with Eleanor. Tuesday is bridge at 1 p.m. at the senior center. Wednesday morning I do the senior center books, about two hours. Wednesday evening is church choir practice though I mostly just listen now. Thursday afternoon I quilt with the quilt guild second and fourth Thursdays at the Methodist church. Friday I grocery shop at Busch's at 9 a.m. and do laundry. Saturday farmers market in summer, library reading hour at 10 a.m. in winter. Sunday church at 9:30, lunch with Kathy at noon, video call with Daniel at 7. Evenings I knit or read or watch a little PBS. Lights out at 9:30.

follow_ups.question: What happens when the schedule gets disrupted?
follow_ups.response: I don't like it. If bridge is canceled I'll feel off the whole day. I've gotten better about it — Harold used to tease me and I try to honor that teasing by loosening up. A little.

follow_ups.question: When do you garden?
follow_ups.response: Every morning May through October, 7 to 8 a.m., after breakfast. That's non-negotiable.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I don't work for pay. I retired from keeping house — if you can call it retiring — when the last kid left, and Harold and I lived on his Ford pension and Social Security. Now I volunteer. The senior center — I do their bookkeeping, reconcile the checkbook, track grant spending, prep the monthly report for the board. That's about eight hours a week, Wednesday mornings plus a bit on Friday afternoon. The library — I help with Saturday morning reading hour for the preschoolers, that's about two hours. And the church — I organize the fellowship meetings twice a month and I'm still treasurer of the United Methodist Women, which I've done since 1996. So about fifteen to eighteen hours a week of volunteer work. Keeps me sharp.

follow_ups.question: How did you get into the senior center bookkeeping?
follow_ups.response: They had a forty-dollar discrepancy in 2021 that nobody could find and I volunteered to look. Found it in an hour — a transposed entry. They asked me to stay on. I couldn't say no.

follow_ups.question: Would you take a paid job if offered?
follow_ups.response: No. The whole point is it's volunteer. If they paid me I'd feel obligated. I like choosing to show up.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I take care of the yard — mow it myself with the self-propelled, rake leaves, shovel the front walk though Kathy's made me promise to hire someone for the driveway after I slipped in January 2024. I handle my own finances, I pay all the bills online now though I still write out a check register in a spiral notebook because I don't trust the computer. I do Ellen's mail and dog when she travels, maybe four, five times a year. I make a double batch of whatever I cook and freeze half for the church's meals ministry. And I write actual letters — I send two or three cards or letters a week, birthday cards for every grandchild and grandniece, thank-you notes, that kind of thing.

follow_ups.question: How did the January 2024 slip go?
follow_ups.response: Bruised my hip, no break, thank the Lord. Kathy was fit to be tied. I now have a fellow named Rob who plows for forty dollars a storm. It galled me to pay for something I could do.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: I hired Rob for the plowing this winter, as I said. I added a Zoom session with the senior center grant committee on the first Thursday of the month — they wanted me on it and I said only if I don't have to drive at night. And my walking pace has slowed, Eleanor and I used to do three miles and now we do two. Otherwise the routine is what it's been for five years.

follow_ups.question: How did you learn Zoom?
follow_ups.response: My grandson Brian walked me through it on a video call in 2020. I still have his handwritten cheat sheet taped to the side of the monitor.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Oh, my children are grown — the youngest is fifty-seven. But when they were in school, a weekday was up at six-thirty, Harold gone to the plant by seven, kids had oatmeal and toast, walked to Saline Elementary at eight. Kathy did girl scouts and played flute in band. Daniel did Boy Scouts and ran track. Rebecca did 4-H — she kept a rabbit — and played clarinet. Dinner at six sharp, homework at the kitchen table, bath, bed by nine. Sunday was church, Wednesday was prayer meeting, Saturday was chores. Predictable as a clock.

follow_ups.question: Was the schedule as rigid then as it is now?
follow_ups.response: Oh, more so. Three kids needed it. I wrote the week's meals on a chalkboard in the kitchen every Sunday night.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very little, and all positive. Saline officers come to the senior center for a coffee meet-and-greet once a quarter. I got one speeding ticket in 1978 on M-52 outside Chelsea, deserved it. When Harold had his heart attack in 2019 a Saline officer got there before the ambulance and did CPR — couldn't save him but he tried. I sent him a card. That's my experience with law enforcement.

follow_ups.question: Do you know any officers personally?
follow_ups.response: Officer Davis who comes to the senior center — his mother is in my bridge group's substitute list. It's a small town.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The break-in attempt in 1987 — an officer came out at 2 a.m., took a report, very professional. And the accident in 1993 when Daniel rear-ended someone on US-12, the state trooper was kind to him, he was shaken.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No one close to me has been arrested. My nephew on Harold's side had a DUI in the late nineties and did a weekend in the Washtenaw jail. That's it.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: Every election since 1962. Primary, general, school board, millage — every one. I've missed maybe two out of roughly a hundred and twenty elections in my life, both when I had the flu. I consider it an obligation. My mother voted in 1920 the year women got the vote, she told me that story a hundred times, and I am not going to be the one to break the chain.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever worked the polls?
follow_ups.response: Yes — I was an election worker in Saline's precinct 3 for eight cycles, 2004 through 2018. I liked the paperwork.

follow_ups.question: Absentee or in-person?
follow_ups.response: In-person, always, but I went absentee in 2020 because of COVID and in 2022 and 2024 because standing in line got harder. I drop the ballot at the clerk's office myself.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'm what they used to call a Rockefeller Republican — fiscally careful, socially a little more live-and-let-live than people assume. I was a Republican for most of my life, voted for Eisenhower in spirit before I could vote, then Nixon in '68 and '72, Ford, Reagan, both Bushes. I voted for Obama in 2008 — that surprised me as much as anyone, but I'd soured on the Iraq war and the financial crisis and John McCain picking Sarah Palin was the last straw. I registered as an independent in 2016 and I have not voted for a Republican for president since. I voted for Clinton in 2016, Biden in 2020, Harris in 2024. For local and state offices I still split the ticket — I voted for the Republican county clerk because she runs a tight office. On issues, I'm for balanced budgets, against waste, for strong public schools and libraries, for Social Security and Medicare being left alone, for gun laws that require background checks and training, I am not comfortable with the extremes on either side but I have been more alarmed by the Republican direction since 2016. I'm pro-choice, privately, though I don't talk about it at church. I believe gay people should be married — my own son is. I think immigrants built this country including my grandfather. I think the environment is a gift we were supposed to steward. I was raised to believe that a person's word was their bond and that's gotten scarce in politics. I don't like what it's become.

follow_ups.question: What was the Obama vote like for you?
follow_ups.response: I surprised myself in the booth. I stood there a long time. I remember thinking my grandfather Otto would have understood, he was an immigrant and a trade unionist before he quit speaking German.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with friends?
follow_ups.response: Selectively. Marjorie is a lifelong Democrat and we talk. Pat in bridge is MAGA and we don't. I've learned to say 'well, we won't settle it today' and change the subject.

follow_ups.question: What about with family?
follow_ups.response: Daniel and Kathy are on my side of things. Rebecca's husband Greg voted for Trump all three times and Rebecca is quieter about her views. We agreed at Thanksgiving 2016 not to discuss it at the table and we've kept that.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: The biggest change is I no longer trust the Republican party as an institution, and I used to. That shift started with the Tea Party in 2010 and became permanent in 2016. I've also shifted left on some social things as I've aged, which people don't expect — I'm more comfortable with the changes in gender roles and family structure than I was at forty. Having Daniel and Marco and watching their life helped. I'm also more worried about democracy itself than I used to be. I watch the news with a knot in my stomach I didn't have in 1988. That's new.

follow_ups.question: What news do you watch?
follow_ups.response: PBS NewsHour at 6 p.m., and the Sunday morning shows, mostly Meet the Press and Face the Nation. I read the Ann Arbor News online and the Saline Reporter in print.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever change the channel to a conservative outlet to hear the other side?
follow_ups.response: I used to read the Wall Street Journal opinion page. I still sometimes. I don't watch Fox — I find it not serious.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat, I'd say honestly. I grew up in an all-white small town, my whole life has been mostly white spaces, and I was raised in a time when people said things I now understand were wrong. The George Floyd video in 2020 shook me. I watched it twice and I cried. I thought about my own children and what if an officer had done that to Daniel. I don't think that gives me any particular standing but it did change how I listen. I've become more willing to hear Black friends and my grandson Brian's wife — she's Black, from Atlanta — talk about things I would have dismissed twenty years ago.

follow_ups.question: How did your grandson's marriage affect your thinking?
follow_ups.response: Brian married Keisha in 2021, she's a wonderful woman, pediatrician. Watching them navigate things as a couple, watching her parents at the wedding and talking with her mother — you learn. I wasn't the one learning it the hard way, she was.

follow_ups.question: Have you talked with Keisha about BLM directly?
follow_ups.response: Once, at Christmas 2021, carefully. I asked her what she thought and I listened. She was gracious with me. I tried not to make her do the work of teaching me — I've read some on my own.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core point — that Black Americans experience policing differently and that we should take that seriously — is correct. I'm less sure about some of the policy specifics, defund the police as a slogan did not land right with me, I want good policing and better-trained policing. I think accountability and transparency are the right frame. I also think the work is generational and none of this gets fixed in one news cycle.

follow_ups.question: Have you donated or joined anything?
follow_ups.response: I donated to the Washtenaw County NAACP in 2020 and 2021. I haven't joined a group. I'm eighty-five, my activism looks like voting and writing a check.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I'm worried. I feel like we took steps forward and then steps back. I worry about what my grandchildren Brian and Keisha's future children will face. I think white people my age have an obligation to say out loud that this matters, because the young folks saying it get dismissed, and I think our silence over the decades is part of why we're where we are.

follow_ups.question: Do you say it out loud?
follow_ups.response: More than I used to. In bridge, in fellowship group, when it comes up. Carefully. I'm not a pulpit person.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Family and friends, and the checkbook. I haven't been to a protest — my knees wouldn't let me — but I have talked about it with my children and grandchildren, and with Marjorie and Eleanor.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Mixed. Daniel and Marco are deep in it, they march, they donate, they talk. Kathy follows and thinks about it, she's a retired teacher. Rebecca is quieter on it. Greg, Rebecca's husband, thinks it's overblown — we disagree and we've agreed not to argue. Marjorie is engaged. Pat from bridge finds the whole thing irritating — she thinks the country overcorrected. Eleanor and I talk about it fairly often on walks. So it's a cross-section.

follow_ups.question: Has it caused rifts?
follow_ups.response: Not rifts. Tensions that we manage. I'm eighty-five, I pick my battles.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: All things considered, decent for eighty-five. I have high blood pressure, diagnosed in 1998, controlled on lisinopril 20 milligrams. Type 2 diabetes since 2012, controlled with metformin and diet — my last A1C was 6.8. Osteoarthritis in both knees and the right hip, I manage it with Tylenol and walking. I had cataract surgery on both eyes in 2022, night driving is still not great. I'm a little hard of hearing in the left ear, I wear hearing aids at church and bridge. I had a bout with breast cancer in 2005, stage 1, lumpectomy and radiation, clear ever since. Mammogram every year, I'm due in May. I take a multivitamin, vitamin D, calcium, and a baby aspirin. I weigh about a hundred and forty, five-three, down from five-five — I've lost an inch and a half since sixty.

follow_ups.question: Who is your primary doctor?
follow_ups.response: Dr. Patricia Nguyen at the Saline clinic, IHA network. I've been with her since 2016, when Dr. Hendricks retired.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about the diabetes?
follow_ups.response: Managed but I respect it. I don't eat sweets the way I used to. Kathy got me a CGM through Medicare last year and I check it every morning.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: the routine — I walk twice a week, I garden, I cook my own food, I don't drink more than a glass of wine a month. My weight is steady. My doctor is good and I take my medications at 7:15 every morning. Hard: the knees, the eyes, the fact that I live alone and cooking for one is hard to do right. And winter — four months of not being outside much, I can feel the difference by March.

follow_ups.question: What do you eat in a typical day?
follow_ups.response: Oatmeal and berries and coffee for breakfast. A small salad and a piece of chicken or a cup of soup for lunch. Dinner is a real meal — pot roast, fish, chicken, with a vegetable from the garden or the freezer. A square of dark chocolate after.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The slip on the ice in January 2024 — bruised hip, no break, three weeks of soreness. My A1C crept up in summer 2024 and we added five more milligrams of metformin. I had a bad cold in November 2025 that turned into bronchitis, prednisone and amoxicillin fixed it in ten days. A skin tag removed from my back at dermatology in March 2025, benign. Otherwise no hospitalizations, no emergencies. I knock on wood.

follow_ups.question: Was the slip a wake-up call?
follow_ups.response: Yes. That's when I hired Rob for the driveway and started using a cane on icy days. I hate the cane but I use it.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My volunteering has had to adjust. I used to do four hours at the library and I'm down to two. I quilt shorter sessions because my hands cramp — I do ninety minutes at a go instead of three hours. Otherwise I get where I need to get.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Harold, of course — his heart attack in 2019 was sudden, he was gone before the ambulance got there. My sister Maggie has early-stage Alzheimer's, diagnosed 2023. She still lives alone in Tecumseh but her daughter is making plans. Our Tuesday and Friday calls — she repeats herself more than she used to. That's hard. Kathy had a breast cancer scare in 2020, turned out benign, thank God. Rebecca's back surgery in 2021. Nothing catastrophic recently.

follow_ups.question: How do you handle Maggie's repetitions?
follow_ups.response: I don't correct her. I just answer the question again. She was my first friend in the world, she's allowed to forget.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Medicare with a supplemental plan — Blue Cross Plan G — and Part D for drugs. It works well. My out-of-pocket is predictable. I've never forgone care. Getting appointments is slower than it used to be, dermatology took four months. The IHA system is good and Dr. Nguyen answers the MyChart messages within a day. I feel lucky. Harold and I saved for this.

follow_ups.question: What's your monthly premium?
follow_ups.response: Around two-sixty for the supplemental and forty-five for Part D. Plus what comes out of Social Security for Part B. Maybe four hundred total, roughly.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Not really, not seriously. My mother swore by ginger tea for nausea and I still make it. I use a heating pad for the knees. I tried acupuncture once in 2010 for my shoulder, it helped, I didn't go back. I don't take herbals because I'm careful about interactions with my blood pressure medicine. I respect it but I don't use it.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I've never smoked. Harold smoked for twenty years and quit in 1979, cold turkey after his father died of lung cancer. I drink very lightly — a glass of wine at Thanksgiving and Christmas, maybe one with Kathy on her birthday. I don't cope by drinking. After Harold died I had a glass of sherry on my worst nights for a few weeks and then I stopped because I didn't like the pattern of it.

follow_ups.question: Anyone in the family struggle with it?
follow_ups.response: My uncle Walter, my mother's brother, was a drinker. He died of cirrhosis in 1982. It made an impression on me.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: No. I take Tylenol for the knees — extra strength, two tablets, maybe three times a week. I've never used marijuana. I was offered it in 2020 for the knees by my nephew and declined. I don't take anything for sleep or mood. I've never been on an antidepressant, though I think less of people who are, not at all — Daniel takes one, and my granddaughter Sophie does, and it's the right thing for them.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Medicare and the supplemental cover mine fully, and I have savings. My children all have their own insurance through work or retirement. Nobody in my immediate family is struggling with medical bills right now. I know it's not like this for a lot of people and I'm grateful.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm fully on board. Flu shot every October, pneumonia vaccine, shingles, Tdap boosters. Four COVID vaccines — original in March and April of 2021, booster that fall, updated boosters in 2022 and 2023. I believe in vaccines. My mother saw polio in her town, I saw measles. It's not complicated for me.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Dr. Nguyen. The CDC website, I know how to navigate it. PBS NewsHour. My daughter Kathy who reads a lot of this stuff. Consumer Reports. I do not trust Facebook chain letters and I've said so to one or two people at church who sent them.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Steady, mostly. The grief for Harold isn't sharp anymore, it's a low hum. I have good days and harder days. Winter is harder, spring I come back. The garden coming up in April lifts me. I get some loneliness in the evenings — Winston helps, so does the phone. I feel useful, which matters at my age — the senior center books, the library reading hour, the fellowship group, the grandchildren. I worry about Maggie and what's coming for her. I worry about the country. But on my own scale, I'm content.

follow_ups.question: What does contentment look like for you?
follow_ups.response: A finished crossword, a pot of soup on the stove, the dishes done, a chapter of a book before bed. Small.

follow_ups.question: When was the last time you truly laughed?
follow_ups.response: Sunday — Kathy told me Winston pushed a tomato off the counter and sat on it. I laughed till I cried.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: February 2025, the anniversary week of Harold's death approached — actually it's in September, but February is when I miss him most because of the house being closed up and the cold. I had a stretch of about ten days where I didn't want to get up. I ate oatmeal and that was about it. Kathy noticed and came up and stayed two nights and we cleaned out his workshop — we'd put it off six years. Crying, laughing, boxing things up for Goodwill. After that I came back to myself. It was the right thing to do.

follow_ups.question: Had you talked to anyone professionally during that stretch?
follow_ups.response: No. I'm of a generation that mostly doesn't. I probably should have. I talked to Pastor Jim afterward and he was helpful.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have had bouts of what I'd probably call depression, especially after Harold died, and some seasonal low mood in February every year. I have not been formally diagnosed and I've never taken medication for it. I have mild anxiety about health decline and about driving, and I have a small amount of generalized worry that runs in the background. On the whole I'd say I'm a worrier but a functional one.

follow_ups.question: Would you consider talking to a therapist?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, yes, I've thought about it more the last two years. The senior center has a social worker who does free sessions. I've considered it.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Daniel has been open about his depression since college and takes an SSRI, he's steady. Sophie my granddaughter has anxiety, she's in therapy and it helps her. Rebecca had postpartum depression after Lily in 2009, she got help and came through. We're a family that has it and manages it.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Important, quietly. I've been a United Methodist my whole life. Saline First United Methodist since 1964. I go Sunday at 9:30, I'm in the fellowship group, I was on the finance committee for twelve years and I'm still treasurer of the UMW. I pray in the morning with my coffee and at night before bed, nothing elaborate, mostly gratitude and petition for people. I read the Bible most mornings, I'm in Psalms right now. My faith is not showy, I don't proselytize, I don't like the political weaponization of religion that's happening. I believe in a God who is love, I believe Jesus meant what he said about the poor and the stranger, and I try to live as if that's true. I think of faith as practice more than belief. Show up, help, be decent, forgive when you can.

follow_ups.question: Has your faith changed as you've aged?
follow_ups.response: Less certain about the details, more certain about the essentials. I used to argue theology, I don't anymore. I still believe in resurrection, though I hold it lightly.

follow_ups.question: Did faith help after Harold?
follow_ups.response: Yes. The church ladies brought casseroles for three weeks. The liturgy held me up when I couldn't think. I sat in the pew and let the words carry me.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I have Facebook, joined in 2011 because Rebecca made me. I check it once a day, usually after lunch. I look at pictures of grandchildren, I wish people happy birthday, I post maybe once a month — a picture of the garden, a quilt I finished. I'm in two groups, the Saline Senior Center group and a quilting group out of Ypsilanti. I don't have Instagram. I have an iPhone and I text with my children. I don't do Twitter, TikTok, any of that. I use email — I have a Gmail account, I check it morning and evening. Zoom for the senior center meeting and for the grandkids when they won't FaceTime.

follow_ups.question: Has Facebook ever caused problems?
follow_ups.response: A cousin of Harold's gets political and I hid her posts. One of the ladies at church shares things I know are false and I've told her privately I wish she'd check.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever buy anything through social media?
follow_ups.response: Never. I don't trust it. I buy off actual store websites — I order fabric from Missouri Star Quilt Company.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: No. I ask for help in person or on the phone. Facebook's not where I go for comfort. After Harold died I got beautiful comments on the memorial post but the real support was the casseroles and the visits.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress is higher than it was five years ago — the news, Maggie's diagnosis, my own creep of health issues. I cope by sticking harder to the routine, by walking with Eleanor, by calling Marjorie, by quilting. I've added a 3 p.m. cup of tea and ten minutes of sitting quietly in the sunroom. That's a new ritual.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: Just me and Winston the cat.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Just me. House is paid off since 1999.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Property tax installment — about eight hundred. Medicare supplemental and Part D about three-ten. Utilities about two-twenty — gas, electric, water, internet. Groceries about three-fifty. Gas for the car maybe forty. Car insurance eighty-five. Homeowner's insurance about a hundred and twenty monthly equivalent. Charitable giving — tithe to church, about two hundred a month.

follow_ups.question: Do you track every expense?
follow_ups.response: Every penny. Spiral notebook and a spreadsheet, I reconcile them monthly. Harold taught me that and I kept it up.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: Last month was about twenty-four hundred, which is typical. A heavy month — property tax, vet visit for Winston, new quilting fabric — runs thirty-two hundred. A light month with no extras is nineteen hundred. I average around twenty-three hundred.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: Own, free and clear since 1999. We paid off the mortgage the year Rebecca finished college.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Winter gas bills run two-fifty a month December through February, down to forty in July. Property tax hits in July and December. Homeowner's insurance renews in May, I pay annual — fourteen hundred last year. Car insurance semi-annually in April and October. Christmas gifts for the grandchildren, I budget six hundred. Birthdays spread through the year, another four hundred total. Medical runs higher in the quarter when I have my checkups. Garden supplies peak in April, maybe a hundred fifty. I plan all of it in a spreadsheet at the beginning of January.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: The furnace motor went out in November, three-eighty to repair. I paid from the emergency fund in savings and replenished over two months by cutting the fabric budget. That's how I cope — I don't use credit.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: I save. I have a money market account at Bank of Ann Arbor with about forty-two thousand as my emergency fund and general savings. I have a brokerage account at Vanguard with the bulk of what Harold and I accumulated — I'm not going to give a number but it's enough that I take required minimum distributions and give the rest to charity through a donor-advised fund to keep taxes reasonable. I have CDs at Chase, a ladder. I save about two hundred a month from my Social Security and pension into the money market.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Rainy day, and legacy. I don't have a big thing to save for — no new roof coming yet, no trip I'm saving for. I save for emergencies and because I want something left for the children and grandchildren. I've told them I'd rather give some of it while I'm alive, I've been doing the annual gift tax exclusion amount to each of them for three years now.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: None. I pay the credit card in full every month. House paid off. Car paid off — 2019 Honda CR-V, paid cash with a trade-in. No debt.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: There hasn't been such a time. I'm fortunate. I know that's not the answer most people give.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My paid occupation, looking back, is homemaker, though I kept the books for Harold's side small-engine repair business from 1966 to 1992, which was a few hundred dollars a month of 1099 income. In the Census I'd put 'not in workforce' since retirement. What I do now that looks like work is volunteer bookkeeping — I reconcile the senior center's checking and money market accounts monthly, I categorize expenses against their grant accounts, I prepare the monthly financial report for the board. I use QuickBooks Online since 2022, before that it was spreadsheets. For the church's UMW I keep the treasurer's books, simpler, probably thirty transactions a month. Reading hour at the library is a two-hour shift, prepping the books, reading aloud to preschoolers, singing. Event coordination for church fellowship — planning the menu, the space, the program, and following up.

follow_ups.question: What was your peak paid income?
follow_ups.response: From Harold's books I never made more than about three thousand a year, 1980s dollars. I wasn't the earner.

follow_ups.question: Do you consider yourself retired?
follow_ups.response: Officially, yes. Functionally, I put in about twenty hours of real work a week. It just isn't paid.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No. Homemaker. Harold was UAW at Ford's Ypsilanti plant — Local 898, I think — and his pension is union-negotiated and it has supported me since he died.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: Zero weeks of paid work.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Zero paid. About eighteen to twenty volunteer.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: No paid jobs.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Zero paid jobs.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: Zero from jobs. My income comes from Harold's Ford pension — about twenty-seven hundred a month — and Social Security survivor benefit plus my own, about nineteen-fifty a month. Plus modest investment income. So maybe fifty-five hundred gross a month, a bit more with RMD distributions.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Monthly — pension the first, Social Security the third Wednesday.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: About fifty-five hundred gross, depending on the month. My household is just me.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, tax year 2024, filed in March 2025. I use an accountant in Ann Arbor, Richard Beauchamp, he's done our taxes since 1988. He charges me two-fifty. I'll never switch.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: No paid workplace. Senior center volunteer five years, library three years. No benefits, and I don't want any.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: At the senior center I report to the director, Linda Alvarez, we get along. Co-volunteers are friends. No conflict to speak of.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Perfectly predictable because I volunteer and I set the days. Wednesday morning senior center, Saturday morning library, second and fourth Sundays fellowship. I'm flexible because I choose not to be — I keep the same hours so people can find me.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not applicable now — my children are grown. When they were little I didn't work for pay.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No. Medicare and Social Security only.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: My income doesn't fluctuate. Pension and Social Security are fixed. I can't remember a tight month in the last year.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: I'd pay it from the money market without blinking. The furnace in November was three-eighty and that's essentially what it was. Emergency fund is there on purpose.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Secure, grateful, and aware that this is not the norm for a lot of my friends. Harold and I lived below our means for fifty-eight years. We paid off the house early, we maxed out what we could into his 401k once Ford offered it in the eighties, we didn't take vacations we couldn't pay cash for. I've got enough that I can give and not worry. I feel blessed. I also know luck was part of it — Harold's union job, the house appreciating, Social Security and Medicare being there. A lot of people worked just as hard as we did and ended up with less because the ground under them moved.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever feel guilty about having more than others?
follow_ups.response: Not guilty. Aware. That's why I tithe and give. I think people who have should give.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: Widowed. Harold passed September 14, 2019. Not living with anyone, no romantic partner. I don't expect one at eighty-five.

follow_ups.question: Have you dated at all?
follow_ups.response: No. A gentleman from church asked me to coffee in 2022, very nice man, I declined. I'm not interested.

transcript.question_text: For our records, we also need your date of birth. Could you please provide that?
Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Yes, born in the United States.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Adrian, Michigan.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: No. The Cintron is from Harold's side — his mother was Puerto Rican, his father German — but I'm not Hispanic by ancestry. I'm German and English.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: White.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: Some college — two years at Siena Heights, no degree. Plus one night class at Washtenaw Community in 1974.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: Not right now. Thinking about it.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No. Harold served in the Army Reserves, 1959 to 1965.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Christian, United Methodist.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: Independent, leaning Democratic for federal races since 2016. I re-registered as independent in 2016. I'd say I lean moderately — not strongly — toward the Democrats now, and I split the ticket for state and local. If the Republican Party returned to what it was I'd consider going back but I don't see that happening.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Democratic, currently. That would have been an unthinkable sentence for me to say in 1992.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Adrian, Michigan.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, both. They were married until my father's death in 1974.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My three younger siblings — Maggie, Paul, and Raymond. And my grandmother Elsa, my mother's mother, lived with us from 1953 until she died in 1961.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: Eighth grade.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: High school, 1933.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, during the war — 1942 to 1945.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She was a riveter at the Willow Run bomber plant — yes, a real Rosie. She took the bus from Adrian to Ypsilanti, rode an hour each way, three shifts rotating. She riveted wing panels on B-24 Liberators. My grandmother watched us. She was proud of that work her whole life and kept her Willow Run ID card in her dresser.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: Ford Motor Company's Willow Run bomber plant. They built B-24 Liberator bombers for the war, at peak a plane an hour. Biggest factory building in the world at the time.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, his entire adult life.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Machine operator at Bohn Aluminum and Brass in Adrian, 1938 to 1969. He ran a die-cast machine that made aluminum parts for cars — mostly transmission housings. Shift work, union man, UAW.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: Bohn Aluminum and Brass Corporation, Adrian plant. Aluminum castings for the automotive industry, primarily Detroit Three customers.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: At eighty-five you hope for time. I hope to be in this house for at least five more years, independent, driving during the day, keeping the garden. I hope to finally finish the business administration certificate at Washtenaw — that's unfinished business for me. I hope to see Sophie become a doctor and Emma become a nurse and Brian and Keisha have a baby and Lily graduate high school. I hope Daniel and Marco come east more often. I hope Maggie stays herself long enough for us to have a few more good visits. I hope the country pulls itself together. I hope when my time comes it's quick, and I hope I have the good sense to go to hospice and not drag it out. I hope I leave my children enough and my grandchildren a head start. I hope I'm remembered as someone who paid attention and showed up.

follow_ups.question: Are you afraid of dying?
follow_ups.response: Not much. I'm afraid of being a burden, and I'm afraid of losing my mind like Maggie's losing hers. I'm not afraid of death itself. I have a faith that carries me on that.

follow_ups.question: What would make the next five years a success?
follow_ups.response: Stay in the house. Finish the certificate. See the grandchildren launched. Keep the garden. Keep the routine. Die in my sleep after a good day.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family. Then my word — that people can count on what I say. Then order — a clean house, a balanced ledger, a garden tended. Then service — I believe we're here to be useful. Then faith — the quiet kind, not the loud kind. Harold told me once I had four values on a three-by-five card and I couldn't argue with him. I'd add a fifth now: perspective. Knowing what's a small thing and what's a big thing.

follow_ups.question: If you had to cut to one, what would it be?
follow_ups.response: Family. Everything else is in service of that.
